questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Personal connection to the destination (heritage / friends there/ etc.)

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: This was my first time back in Vancouver since I moved to Denmark when I was almost three years old. I had been dreaming about an opportunity to go back like this one for as long as I can remember. I didn't know anybody over there, which helped taking it like a "fresh start" and making my own connections.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: They have great exchange coordinators that are easily available, quick and very helpful. Once you get to campus, there are signs everywhere to find the main buildings like the front desk for housing or the dining commons, as well as flyers for upcoming activities during the introductory week.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Again, the exchange coordinators were a great help. There are a lot of volunteers scattered around that are there to help with anything. Worst case, just ask anyone, people are very open and easy to approach, so don't be scared.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
For on campus housing you can choose between residences and townhouses. Residences are dorms with shared washrooms, laundry rooms and a mandatory meal plan for the dining commons. They have common areas on every floor with some amenities like microwaves and sinks. I stayed in Courtyard Residence, which has a common area on the ground floor with stovetops, ovens and microwaves, and one on every floor with microwaves and sinks. Most residences look alike in terms of facilities, it's up to you to get a feel for what you want by looking at their website. 
Then you have townhouses, which are four-bedroom houses with shared kitchens and washrooms. This means that you stay with three roommates. You don't get a mandatory meal plan, but you can make your own food, and it doesn't mean you don't have access to the dining commons. 
There is also Hamilton Hall, which is exclusively for Msc. students, where you get your own apartment, with your own kitchen, washroom etc.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: If you choose to stay in one of the Residences, you automatically get the meal plan, which grants you unlimited access to the dining commons. They have a great variety of food, and hold themselves to a pretty high standard. I'm not saying it's Michelin level, but you don't get tired of what you're eating over the course of a semester. It is a mix between a buffet and food stations (think ramen/curry/pasta bar, rice/noodle bowls etc.), which have weekly rotations and some special events, so look out for those because they're usually pretty great.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer:
I stayed at Courtyard Residence, which is one of the newest buildings with great facilities. The only downside I can think of is that most of the students staying there are first-years, and that it was on the other side of the DC compared to the other residences. Most of the friends I made over there were at the other residences, which made it a little bit socially challenging for me (but I wouldn't worry about that). 
What you should know is that living on campus is great. This was all very new to me, but it is to most students over there as well, so there is this kind of mutual understanding which makes for great conversation starters.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Whether you want to stay in a residence or in a townhouse, I cannot recommend the dining commons enough. First of all, the food is great, not extraordinary but it gets by very well. Second of all, the social impact it has on everybody is exceptional. Everything that will happen during your stay at SFU will spark from an idea shared around a table in there; and it doesn't matter whether it comes from a new best friend or someone you just met 30 seconds ago. That is how I got to see the northern lights in Yellowknife with some friends, or how I spent a week in Hawaii with practically strangers. So yeah, highly recommend the dining commons because of the social impact it had on me.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: The process is a little tedious in terms of gathering documents. But everything is well described during the exchange meeting at UCPH and on the mobility website. Once you are approved for the exchange, you get into contact with the exchange coordinators at SFU who will help guide you through their systems and give you all the information you need.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The exchange coordinators at SFU are readily available by e-mail, just mind the time difference if you need a quick answer.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I got most of the courses I wanted. I had to compromise a little because of some schedule conflicts and some prerequisites I didn't have, but other than that I was pretty satisfied.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There isn't much to worry about since as an exchange student, you are on the priority list for course enrollment. Having said that, I wouldn't wait too long to give them a list of the courses you're interested in taking. If there any problems or requirements you missed, the coordinators will let you know and ask for additional information if needed, so you don't have to worry much about all details.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They have big variety of courses which are mostly available to anyone, except for some like in Computer Science, where you have to be in that major to be able to take some.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I only had 300 level courses, so third year courses for students doing their Bsc.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: They are very similar overall. The classes were a bit smaller, which helps making it a bit more personal between the students and professors.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
MATH 340 Algebra II: Rings and Fields
MATH 322 Complex Variables (or Introduction to Complex Analysis as the professor liked to call it)
PHYS 384 Methods of Theoretical Physics I
NUSC 341 Introduction to Radiochemistry

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I enjoyed Complex Variables, as it was a nice continuation to Analysis 0 and 1 I took at UCPH. It was definitely an "introduction" to complex analysis, as it wasn't as hard as An0 and An1.

Housing DKK per month *

Local transportation DKK per month *
Food DKK per month *
Personal spending DKK per month *

Other fees DKK per month *
What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: You could say the trips I went on could be a part of that category. I put 1500 DKK in other fees as an average per month on trips I participated in over the course of my exchange. Hawaii was not that cheap, but I would take it into account for that average.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I feel like the cost of living in Vancouver is a little bit cheaper that it is in Copenhagen, or that the prices were pretty much the same.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: They have pretty much anything you could think of, from hiking to DnD to volunteering.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend the hiking club, which is an easy way to meet new people and to go on hikes (since apparently that's what people look forward to the most going to Vancouver). I got to play basketball, squash, tennis, badminton, and even got to boulder.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Do most of the hikes early in the semester for the best weather possible. There are a bunch of recommended places all over the internet, I would suggest them all honestly. Go to Whistler at least once, on or off skiing season. Visit Gas Town, Stanley Park, Granville Island, Kitsilano etc. 
Now, you won't get a whole week of holidays like at UCPH, but some days off for like Thanksgiving for example. That's where you should plan big trips like Vancouver Island or Whistler. But nothing stops you from going a bit crazier stuff like Banff, Yellowknife, San Francisco, Hawaii for more than a few days, like a week (but you didn't hear that from me).

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: There is nothing culturally that stands out of the ordinary coming from a European. Just be ready for some small talk with anyone, and thank the bus driver.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: I'll be honest, it is easier to make friends with other exchange students that it is with local students. Local students will mostly be studying, because that is what they're there to do. I'm not saying it is impossible and that they're terrible people, just that they will be less open to spontaneity compared to other students on exchange, because they need to study, and they most likely don't have the money anyway. Locals are very nice and helpful, you can always find them in common areas, the library or in the dining commons.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: It's a small adjustment but tipping and taxes would throw me off more often than not. If you want a culturally rich experience during your exchange, make friends with other exchange students. My most eye-opening cultural exchange was when I went to Yellowknife with some new friends from East-Asia.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Canadians live up to the kind stereotype. They are very open and well-intended people.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: I wouldn't consider myself as an outgoing and talkative person, I am more of the awkward type. But I am barely exaggerating when I say that I greeted everybody I crossed paths with while I was in Vancouver. There is a very freeing sentiment when you first arrive in a new place all on your own, which helps kind of reinventing yourself (not in a bad way). I would embrace that feeling, because I'm sure everyone there thinks the same. This might come off as bad advice but, I would put studying to the side a little, and try to experience as much as possible. Say yes to every opportunity that arises (which most likely will come from the dining commons). I must have spent a maximum of 3 weekends staying on campus, which goes to show that there is a lot of stuff to do and that will pop up out of the blue.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: I would just recommend you do your research in due time before applying for SFU, and if do go there, before every trip that you plan on doing.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: It's cliché but making friends. I was headed into that exchange with the mindset of a student that was going to focus during lectures and on getting good grades. But right off the bat I met some interesting and exciting people and that mindset just disappeared. I was definitely not planning on meeting as many people as I have and go on as many trips as I did, but now I can say I went to Hawaii with lifelong friends from all over the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I don't think there was anything particularly challenging during my exchange. Ironically maybe just getting myself to study at least a little bit for the exams.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: I wholeheartedly encourage anyone to go on exchange, because this was wiiild to say the least. If you're at least considering it I wouldn't think twice just go !

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
